opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I find genuinely important, partly because the answer shapes so much of how we think about governance and about where the risks concentrate.

My rough view is that generality has been winning, and I expect it to keep winning at the frontier for a while. The striking empirical lesson of the last several years is that a single large model trained on broad data tends to outperform narrow systems built for a specific task, often even on that task. There's a kind of positive transfer: learning to reason, to code, to read scientific papers, to model other people, all seem to reinforce each other. So the economic gravity pulls toward a few very capable general systems that then get adapted downstream.

That said, I don't think it's a pure story of generality. There are a few forces pushing the other way. One is cost: if you're running billions of queries, you want something smaller, cheaper and faster, so you'll see distillation into specialised models for particular deployment contexts. Another is data access: some domains, like certain areas of biology, materials science, or proprietary industrial processes, depend on data that isn't on the open internet, so you get specialised models, or specialised fine-tunes, built by whoever holds that data. And a third is reliability: in high-stakes settings people may prefer a narrower system whose behaviour they can characterise and verify, over a general one that's more capable but harder to bound.

So the picture I find most plausible is something like a general core with a specialised periphery: a small number of frontier general models that act as the foundation, and then an ecosystem of tools, fine-tunes, and agents built on top of or distilled from them. Increasingly, the general model may itself orchestrate specialised tools, so the line between the two blurs.

Why this matters from a safety and governance perspective: if generality dominates, then capabilities — including dangerous ones — come bundled. You can't easily get a brilliant scientific assistant without also getting something that could help with, say, bioweapons design or cyber offence, unless you do deliberate work to separate them. That puts a lot of weight on the frontier developers, on evaluations, and on things like structured access. It also means power and influence may concentrate in whoever controls those general systems, which raises questions about competition, about accountability, and about international dynamics.

On the other hand, there's an appealing vision, which people like Eric Drexler have articulated in different forms, where we deliberately lean into specialisation, building comprehensive services out of bounded, task-specific systems rather than one agentic generalist. I think there's real wisdom there as a safety strategy. My worry is that it may not be competitive by default, so if we want that world, it probably requires coordination or policy to make it stick, rather than expecting the market to deliver it on its own.

r001.rationale: The response mentions distilling general models into specialised models, but does not propose removing historical knowledge from a coding model or say that history helped it learn to code.

r002.rationale: It says generality has been winning and expects it to keep winning at the frontier for a while, communicating that its benefits have not peaked yet.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of the questions I find most interesting, and I think it's genuinely contested within the field. Let me try to lay out how I think about it.

So the first thing to say is that generality has been the surprising winner of the last decade. If you'd asked most people in 2015 how we'd get to systems that could write code, pass the bar exam, do protein structure prediction, and so on, I think most would have expected a lot of specialised systems, each engineered for its domain. Instead what happened is that scaling up fairly general architectures trained on fairly general objectives, mostly predicting the next token, produced capabilities that transferred across domains in ways nobody really engineered. That's a remarkable fact about the world, and I think we still don't fully understand why it worked as well as it did.

Now, the question is whether that continues. And I think there are a few considerations pulling in different directions.

On the side of generality continuing to dominate: there's this argument that intelligence is in some deep sense about having good general-purpose representations of the world, and once you have those, specialising is cheap. You can fine-tune, you can prompt, you can give the model tools. So the frontier stays general, and specialisation happens as a thin layer on top. Under that view, the economic and strategic value concentrates in whoever builds the best general base, and the specialised applications are almost commoditised downstream.

On the other side, there are real reasons to think specialisation remains valuable, maybe increasingly valuable. One is just economics. Inference costs matter a lot at scale, and if you're running billions of queries for a narrow task, you don't want to pay for a model that also knows medieval poetry. Distillation and smaller specialised models are going to be a big part of the deployment picture. A second is data. In a lot of domains the frontier of capability is going to be set not by general reasoning but by access to proprietary, domain-specific data, whether that's biology, materials, particular industrial processes, and that's naturally going to produce specialised systems. And a third, which I think people underweight, is that in some domains like AlphaFold or the maths systems, you get big gains from domain-specific training signals like verifiable rewards that don't exist in general.

Where I come down is something like: the frontier of capability will probably remain general, in the sense that the most capable systems will be broad ones, and specialisation will mostly be derived from them rather than built independently. But the question that matters for governance and safety isn't just where the frontier is, it's where the value and the risk are. And I think both of those are more distributed than the frontier picture suggests.

From a safety perspective, I'd actually say generality is where most of my concern lives. A specialised system has a fairly well-defined envelope of things it can do and things it can't, which makes it much easier to evaluate, to build guardrails around, to reason about failure modes. A general system is, almost by definition, one whose full set of capabilities you can't enumerate in advance. That's what makes dangerous capability evaluation so hard: you're trying to find out what the system can do, including things nobody intended it to do. So one way of reading the whole safety agenda is as a response to generality specifically.

And then there's a geopolitical dimension. If generality dominates and the frontier is concentrated in a handful of labs, you get a world with a small number of very consequential actors, which is challenging but also potentially tractable for coordination. If specialisation ends up mattering a lot, capability is more diffuse, more actors matter, and the coordination problem looks quite different. I don't think we know yet which world we're in, and I think a lot of good policy involves being robust to both.

So I suppose my honest answer is: I expect generality to keep winning at the frontier, I expect specialisation to matter enormously for deployment and for certain data-rich domains, and I think the more important question for people in my line of work is less "which wins" and more "what does each imply for how you govern these systems."

r002.rationale: The response predicts generality will keep winning at the frontier, but it does not say that returns to generality have not yet peaked.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a real uncertainty here. You can imagine a world in which the economically valuable systems are quite specialised: they’re very good at particular kinds of research, or engineering, or running some business process. And there are good reasons to specialise. You can make a system cheaper, more reliable, and easier to evaluate for the task you actually care about.

But generality has a particular value when you don’t know in advance what capabilities a task will require. If you’re doing research, part of the challenge is figuring out what the problem is, which tools to use, and when to draw on an apparently unrelated field. A general system can potentially do that without a human having to coordinate all the pieces.

And these possibilities aren’t mutually exclusive. You might have a general model that provides the foundation for lots of specialised systems. Or a general system that delegates to specialised tools. So the fact that most applications look specialised wouldn’t necessarily tell us that generality had become less important.

The question I’d want to ask is: where is the bottleneck? Is it executing a well-specified task, or is it deciding what to do and adapting when things change? To the extent that it’s the latter, I would expect generality to remain very valuable. But I’d be cautious about assuming that a single general model will be the best or most economical way to do everything.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose removing or distilling historical knowledge from a coding model.

r002.rationale: It says generality may remain valuable when tasks require adaptation, but does not predict that frontier AI has yet to reach peak returns to generality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are forces pushing in both directions. There’s a lot of value in specialisation: if you know exactly what task you want performed, you can often make a system cheaper and more reliable by tailoring it to that task. And when you’re deploying something millions of times, those efficiency gains matter enormously.

But generality has some advantages that are easy to underestimate. The world doesn’t arrive neatly divided into tasks. Often, to do one thing well, you need to understand a whole range of other things, recognise when you’re outside your competence, and adapt to circumstances that weren’t anticipated. A more general system can also help you figure out what the task should be in the first place.

So I wouldn’t necessarily expect a choice between one general model that does everything and lots of completely separate specialists. You could have a very general model coordinating specialised systems, or general models that are adapted for particular applications. Those possibilities are quite compatible.

The question I’m especially interested in is where the most consequential capabilities come from. Does making a system more general give it qualitatively greater ability to carry out long, complex projects, to do research, to operate in unfamiliar environments? If it does, then generality could remain very important at the frontier, even if most of the actual computation in the economy ends up being devoted to fairly specialised applications. I’m uncertain about how that balance plays out.

r002.rationale: It says generality could remain important at the frontier and expresses uncertainty, but does not predict that frontier AI has not yet reached peak returns to generality.
